redrafts.value: That he was cheerful and talked to everybody.
redrafts.execution: Being cheerful and talking to everybody is Mr Bingley at the ball, at lines 36 and 37: true of him, but from a later part of the passage. From the upper window at lines 7 and 8 the daughters learned only that he wore a blue coat and rode a black horse.

redrafts.value: That he had ten thousand pounds a year.
redrafts.execution: Ten thousand a year is Mr Darcy's, at line 29, carried across to Mr Bingley. From the upper window at lines 7 and 8 the daughters learned only that he wore a blue coat and rode a black horse.

redrafts.value: A ride on Mr Bennet's black horse.
redrafts.execution: The black horse at line 8 is the one Mr Bingley himself rode, carried across to Mr Bennet and turned into something Mr Bingley wanted. Lines 5 and 6 give what he hoped for: a sight of the young ladies.

redrafts.value: He had gone to London to gather a big group for the ball.
redrafts.execution: The London party is Lady Lucas's guess at lines 15 to 17, after the refusal and not part of it. His answer, at line 11, says only that he was obliged to be in town the following day.

redrafts.value: That the girls would have to meet twelve strange ladies.
redrafts.execution: The twelve ladies are at line 18, outside lines 13 to 16, and it is the girls who grieve over them there, not Mrs Bennet. Her fear is at lines 14 and 15: that he might always be flying about and never settled at Netherfield.

redrafts.value: The ball that Mr Bingley talked of giving at Netherfield.
redrafts.execution: Mr Bingley talks of giving a ball at Netherfield at line 38, later in the passage, and the child carries that party-like event back to line 21. At line 21 'party' is the group that entered the assembly-room, counted at lines 21 and 22 as five people.

redrafts.value: Because he danced with lots of different ladies.
redrafts.execution: Dancing every dance is Mr Bingley at line 37, carried across to Mr Darcy, who dances only twice at lines 39 and 40. Lines 27 to 29 give why the room admired Mr Darcy: his fine, tall person and handsome features, and the report of his ten thousand a year.

redrafts.value: Because he owned a large estate in Derbyshire.
redrafts.execution: The Derbyshire estate is at line 33, outside lines 26 to 30, and it is named only after the room has turned against him. Within the window, lines 27 to 29 give his looks and the report of his ten thousand a year.

redrafts.value: He complained that the ball had ended too early.
redrafts.execution: Complaining that the ball closed early is Mr Bingley at line 37, transferred to Mr Darcy. Lines 31 and 32 give what changed the room: his manners, as he was found to be proud and above his company.

redrafts.value: Every dance of the evening.
redrafts.execution: Every dance is Mr Bingley's at line 37, just before the window opens at line 39, carried across to Mr Darcy. Lines 39 and 40 give Mr Darcy only two dances, once with Mrs Hurst and once with Miss Bingley.

redrafts.value: Tell his friend off for being rude about the ladies.
redrafts.execution: The rudeness about the ladies is at lines 55 and 56, in Mr Darcy's reply, after this speech. Mr Bingley's aim is at line 51: 'I must have you dance.'

redrafts.value: A shower of dry leaves blown across the road.
redrafts.execution: The dry leaves blown across the road are at lines 4 and 5, at the start of the journey, outside lines 22 to 24. Within the window, lines 23 and 24 give what fell: an oak, torn up by the roots.

redrafts.value: A line drawn on the wall to work from.
redrafts.execution: The child reuses the mark he made on the wall at lines 34 and 35, but the rule is a separate thing he takes up. At line 38 he takes the rule and re-measures with it, so it is a measuring tool, not a line on the wall.

redrafts.value: By shouting at her to wake up.
redrafts.execution: Roberta does call out 'Wake up! wake up!' at line 4, outside this window, after Phyllis has already stirred and answered at line 3. Line 1 gives how she woke her: by pulling her hair gently.

redrafts.value: She was staying in the house and did not dare.
redrafts.execution: The narrator did not dare at line 24, outside this window, and that was about laughing at the reading, not about this report. Line 50 gives her reason: 'It is said', so she has the story only from others.

redrafts.value: The bundle and the lilacs put in beside her.
redrafts.execution: The bundle and the lilacs are at line 14, outside this window, put in beside her by her mother before the coach set off; they are not a cost. At line 50 Mr Cobb says there is no extra charge to sit by him.

redrafts.value: Go round the cliff and get in front.
redrafts.execution: Going round the cliff to get in front is what Mark does at lines 30 and 31, a long way outside this window, and Bevis never asks for it. At line 1 Bevis asks Mark to fetch his fishing-rod.

redrafts.value: Whether the world has grown smaller.
redrafts.execution: Stuart and Ralph do argue about whether the world has grown smaller, but that starts at line 10, four lines past the end of this window. Within lines 3 to 6 they disagree about where the thief can go: Ralph says at line 3 that no country is safe for him.

redrafts.value: Whether bad weather has been taken into account.
redrafts.execution: Bad weather is Stuart's objection at line 21, after this window, and Fogg answers it at line 23 with 'All included' rather than correcting it. Within the window, Fogg corrects Stuart's 'three months' at line 18 to 'In eighty days' at line 19.

redrafts.value: Four thousand pounds, as Stuart has just done.
redrafts.execution: Stuart wagers four thousand at line 42, three lines before this window opens at line 45, and the child gives Stuart's stake as Fogg's. Fogg's own stake, at lines 45 and 46, is the twenty thousand he has deposited at Baring's.

redrafts.value: One has a post and the other has none.
redrafts.execution: A post is mentioned at line 6, far above this window, where the ball 'goes by the post' and Kieran swears it was in. It is not a difference between the ends: line 31 gives their end proper netting, and line 33 gives ours two jumpers.

redrafts.value: Climb up into the big man’s lap.
redrafts.execution: Climbing up into the big man's lap is at line 32, outside this window, where he goes up to watch the writing. Lines 5 and 6 give what he could do with any leg he chose: scratch himself anywhere he pleased.

redrafts.value: They had gone over in the wind.
redrafts.execution: Going over in the wind is said of Denise's dahlias at lines 7 and 8, outside this window, and these are tomato leaves. Line 13 gives what happened to the tomato leaves: they had curled in on themselves and gone crisp.

redrafts.value: He counted them out loud into the bucket.
redrafts.execution: Counting out loud into the bucket is at line 23, outside this window, and it is the potatoes Grandad counts, not the sandwiches. Lines 35 and 36 give what he did with his sandwich: he got through half and passed the narrator the rest.
